analysis.one_liner: Requires public companies to get shareholder approval for political spending and disclose it.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 16 Democratic cosponsors but never received a committee vote, hearing, or floor action in the Senate before Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend securities law so that a publicly traded company cannot spend money on political ads or electioneering without a majority of its shareholders voting to approve it. It would also require the company's board to vote on any political spending over $50,000 and publish each director's vote within 48 hours, and require quarterly public reports of all political expenditures, including payments to trade associations that could be used for politics. Corporate officers who spent money without approval could be personally liable for three times the amount.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders — including retirement savers whose 401(k)s and mutual funds hold corporate stock — would gain a say over how company money is used in politics, and voters would gain a searchable public record of which companies paid for political ads, including money routed through trade associations.

how_it_helps.text: No company could make an independent expenditure or electioneering communication unless a majority of outstanding shares voted to authorize political spending for that year [S3].
Boards must vote on any political expenditure over $50,000 and publish each director's individual vote within 48 hours, so investors can see who approved the spending [S3].

Companies must file quarterly public reports describing each political expenditure, its date and amount, the candidates supported or opposed, and the names of trade associations or tax-exempt groups receiving dues that could fund political activity [S3].
Officers or directors who authorize unauthorized political spending commit a breach of fiduciary duty and are jointly and severally liable for three times the amount spent [S3].
Institutional investment managers must disclose how they voted on shareholder authorization, and get a safe harbor protecting decisions to divest from companies over their political spending [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporate executives and boards lose unilateral control over political spending, and publicly traded companies bear the cost of proxy votes, quarterly reporting, and website disclosure. Trade associations and 501(c) groups lose the anonymity of corporate dues money that currently flows to them without shareholder knowledge.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires approval by a majority of all outstanding shares — not just votes cast — which is a high bar for companies with dispersed ownership, so it could function as a near-prohibition on most corporate political spending rather than a light-touch disclosure rule [S3].
Treble-damages personal liability for any director who authorizes an unauthorized expenditure creates litigation risk for board members and could chill ordinary governance decisions [S3].

Requiring a separate annual shareholder vote and quarterly reporting adds compliance costs and proxy-season complexity for every registered public company, regardless of how much political spending it does [S3].

Naming trade associations that receive dues could indirectly expose which companies fund 'dark money' groups, a transparency gain for voters but a practical concern for companies that pay dues for other reasons [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: shareholder control and public disclosure of political spending versus new compliance and litigation burdens on public companies. The disclosure and board-vote provisions are modest and hard to object to on their face; the majority-of-all-outstanding-shares requirement and treble-damages liability make this a much stronger intervention than a pure disclosure bill, which is likely why it drew no Republican support. The cost falls on corporate management, not on consumers directly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was filed, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Menendez introduced the bill on March 2, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day [S5].

That referral to committee was the bill's last action of record; there was no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no further action through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 [S5].
Sixteen Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate executives, boards, and trade associations keep spending company money on independent political advertising without shareholder approval, and the names of companies funding political groups through trade-association dues stay off the public record.

industries.industry: Corporate political spending apparatus of public companies
industries.note: The bill would require majority shareholder approval before any independent expenditure or electioneering communication, plus personal treble-damages liability for executives who spend without authorization. Companies lose unilateral control of their political spending, which is precisely the control the bill targets on behalf of shareholders.

Corporate dues and payments that could be used for political activity would need shareholder authorization and would be disclosed by recipient name in quarterly reports. This threatens the anonymity that makes dues-based political funding attractive to companies.

All registered issuers face new proxy-vote, board-vote, and quarterly reporting requirements. The burden is administrative, but the resulting transparency protects the company's own owners and is generally popular with retail investors.

industries.industry: Institutional investment managers (mutual funds and pension managers)
industries.note: Managers subject to Section 13(f) must publicly disclose how they voted on shareholder authorization of political spending, but they receive a legal safe harbor for divesting from companies over their political spending.
